source_text: Proinde extollenda fide centurionis incredibile, si is professus est talem se fidem nec in Israhele inuenisse, ad quem non pertinebat fides Israhelis. sed nec exinde pertinere poterat: adhuc cruda ut probaretur uel compararetur, ne dixerim adhuc nulla? (sed cur non licuerit illi alienae fidei exemplo uti\'? quoniam si ita esset, (dixisset) talem fidem nec in Israhele umquam fuisse. ceterum dicens talem fidem debuisse (se) inuenire in Israhele, *** quique ad hoc uenisset, uti eam inueniret, deus scilicet et Christus Israhelis. quam non suggillasset nisi exactor et sectator eius, aemulus uero etiam maluisset eam talem inuentam, ad quam infirmandam et destruendam magis uenerat, non ad comprobandam. Besuscitauit et mortuum filium uiduae. non nouum documentum. hoc et prophetae creatoris ediderant, quanto magis filius? adeo autem in illud + usque momenti nullum alium deum Christus intulerat, ut omnes illic creatori gloriam retulerint dicentes: magnus prophetes prodiit in nobis, et respexit deus populum suum. quis deus? utique cuius populus et a quo prophetae. quodsi illi quidem creatorem glorificabant, Christus uero et audiens et sciens non corrigebat, et quidem in tanto documento mortui resuscitati creatorem adhuc orantes, sine dubio aut non alium circumferebat deum quam quem in suis beneficiis atque uirtutibus honorari sustinebat, aut quale est, ut illos tam diu errantes sustiueret, ad hoc ueniens, ut errori eorum mederetur? Sed (scandalizatur Iohannes auditis uirtutibus Christi, ut alterius\'. at ego rationem scandali prius expediam, quo facilius haeretici scandalum explodam. ipso iam domino uirtutum, sermone et spiritu patris, operante in terris et praedicante necesse erat portionem spiritus sancti, quae ex forma prophetici moduli in Iohanne egerat praeparaturam uiarum dominicarum, abscedere iam ab Iohanne, redactam scilicet in dominum ut in massalem suam summam. itaque Iohannes, communis iam homo et unus de turba, scandalizabatur quidem, sed qua homo, non qua alium Christum sperans uel intellegens, qui neque (haberet,) unde speraret, ut nihil noui docentem uel operantem. nemo haesitabit de aliquo, quem dum scit non esse nec sperat nec intellegit; Iohannes autem certus erat neminem deum praeter creatorem, uel qua Iudaeus, (ne dicam) etiam prophetes. plane facilius quis haesitabit : de eo, quem cum sciat esse, an ipse sit, nesciat. hoc igitur metu et Iohannes: tu es, inquit, qui uenis, an alium expectamus? simpliciter inquirens, an ipse uenisset, quem expectabat [tu es, qui uenis? id est: qui uenturus es; an alium expectamus? id est: an alius est quem expectamus, si non tu es quem uenturum expectamus?] sperabat enim, sicut omnes opinabantur, ex similitudine documentorum potuisse et prophetam interim missum esse, a quo alius esset, id est maior, qui uenturus expectabatur, ipse scilicet dominus. atque adeo hoc erat Iohannis scandalum, quod dubitabat ipsum uenisse quem expectabant, quem ex praedicatis operationibus agnouisse debuerat. (aut) ut dominus per easdem operationes agnoscendum se nuntiauerit Iohanni? quae cum constent praedicata in Christum creatoris, sicut ad singula ostendimus, satis peruersum, ut Christum non creatoris per ea renuntiarit intellegendum, per quae magis Christum creatoris agnosci compellebat. multo peruersius, si et testimonium Iohanni perhibet non Iohannis Christus, propheten eum confirmans, immo et supra, ut angelum, ingerens etiam scriptum super illo: ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui praeparet uiam tuam, eleganter ad superiorem sensum scandalizati Iohannis commemorans prophetiam, ut confirmans praecursorem Iohannem iam aduenisse extingueret scrupulum interrogationis illius: tu es, qui uenis, an alium expectamus? praecursore enim iam functo officium, praeparata uia domini, ipse erat intellegendus, cui praecursor ministrauerat. maior is quidem omnibus natis mulierum, sed non ideo subiectus ei, qui minor fuerit in regno dei, quasi alterius sit dei regnum, in quo modicus quis maior erit Iohanne, alterius Iohannes, qui omnibus natis mulierum maior sit. siue enim de quocumque dicit modico siue de semetipso per humilitatem, quia minor Iohanne habebatur, omnibus scilicet in solitudinem concurrentibus ad Iohannem potius quam ad Christum, — quid existis uidere in solitudinem? — tantundem est: creatori competit et Iohannem ipsius esse, maiorem natis mulierum, et Christum uel quem(cum)que modicum, qui maior Iohanne futurus sit in regno (dei,) — aeque creatoris — et qui sit maior tanto propheta, quia non fuerit scandalizatus in Christum, quod tunc Iohannem minuit. Diximus de remissa peccatorum. illius autem peccatricis feminae argumentum eo pertinebit, ut cum pedes domini osculis figeret, lacrimis inundaret, crinibus detergeret, unguento perduceret, solidi corporis ueritatem, non phantasma inane tractauerit, et ut peccatricis paenitentia secundum creatorem meruerit ueniam, praeponere solitum sacrificio. sed et si paenitentiae stimulus ex fide acciderat, per paenitentiam ex fide iustificata ab eo audiit: fides tua te saluam fecit, qui per Abacuc pronuntiarat: iustus ex fide sua uiuet.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the faith of the centurion is to be extolled, incredible if he, having professed such faith, had not found it in Israel, to whom the faith of Israel did not pertain. But neither could it pertain from that point on: still untested, so that it might be proven or compared, or shall I say, still non-existent? For if it were so, he would have said that such faith had never been in Israel. But in saying that he ought to have found such faith in Israel, and that he had come for this purpose, to find it, God, namely, and Christ of Israel, whom he would not have envied unless he were the exactor and follower of the same, and even an emulator, who would have wished to find such faith, to weaken and destroy it, rather than to confirm it. He raised the dead son of the widow. This is not a new proof. Even the prophets of the Creator had done this, how much more the Son? So, in that moment, Christ had introduced no other God, so that all there referred the glory to the Creator, saying: A great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people. What God? Certainly, the one whose people they were and from whom the prophets came. If they were glorifying the Creator, and Christ, hearing and knowing, did not correct them, and indeed, in such a great proof of the resurrection of the dead, they were still praying to the Creator, without doubt, Christ was either not carrying another God than the one he allowed to be honored in his benefits and virtues, or, if he were, why did he allow them to err for so long, coming for the purpose of healing their error? But John was scandalized, having heard the virtues of Christ, as if they belonged to another. And I will first explain the reason for the scandal, so that I may more easily explode the scandal of the heretic. Since the Lord himself, with the speech and spirit of the Father, was working on earth and preaching, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit, which had been working in John in the form of a prophetic model, should now depart from John, having been returned to the Lord, as it were, to his own master. And so John, now a common man and one of the crowd, was scandalized, but as a man, not as one who hoped for or understood another Christ, who had nowhere to hope, since he was teaching nothing new. No one will hesitate about someone whom he knows is not and does not hope for or understand; but John was certain that there was no God except the Creator, either as a Jew or even as a prophet. It is easier for someone to hesitate about one whom he knows exists, but does not know if he is the one. This, therefore, was John's fear: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' Simply inquiring, whether he had come, whom he expected. For he hoped, as all thought, that, from the similarity of the proofs, a prophet might have been sent in the meantime, from whom another, greater one, who was expected to come, would be different, namely, the Lord himself. And so this was John's scandal, that he doubted whether the one they expected had come, whom he ought to have recognized from the predicted works. Or did the Lord announce himself to be recognized through those same works? Since these predicted works are consistent with Christ the Creator, as we show in each case, it is quite perverse to think that Christ is not the Creator's through those things by which he is more compelled to be recognized as the Creator's. It is even more perverse if Christ bears witness to John, confirming him as a prophet, and even more, as an angel, and also brings forth the scripture about him: 'Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way,' elegantly recalling the prophecy of the scandalized John, to confirm the forerunner John, who had already come, and to extinguish the scruple of his question: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' For the forerunner had already performed his office, the way of the Lord had been prepared, and he was to be understood as the one to whom the forerunner had ministered. He is indeed greater than all born of women, but not for that reason subject to the one who will be lesser in the kingdom of God, as if the kingdom of God were of another, in which a lesser one will be greater than John, another John, who is greater than all born of women. Whether he says this about anyone or about himself in humility, because he was considered lesser than John, since all were running to John in the wilderness rather than to Christ, — what do you go out to the wilderness to see? — it is the same: it is fitting for the Creator that John is his, greater than all born of women, and Christ, or anyone lesser, who will be greater than John in the kingdom of God, — equally the Creator's — and who will be greater than such a prophet, because he was not scandalized in Christ, which then diminished John. We have spoken about the forgiveness of sins. The argument of that sinful woman will pertain to this, that when she kissed the Lord's feet with kisses, inundated them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, she handled the solid truth of the body, not an empty phantom, and that the penitence of the sinful woman, according to the Creator, merited forgiveness, preferring it to sacrifice. But even if the stimulus of penitence had come from faith, through penitence, justified by faith, she heard from him: 'Your faith has saved you,' who had pronounced through Habakkuk: 'The just will live by his faith.'

pass_b_english: The centurion's faith deserves the highest praise. It would be incredible if he, having declared such faith, had not found its equal in Israel — especially since the faith of Israel was not even his concern. Nor could it have become his concern at that point: it was still raw, awaiting proof or comparison — or shall I say, still non-existent? If it had existed, he would have claimed that such faith had never appeared in Israel at all. Yet by saying he ought to have found such faith in Israel, and that he came precisely to find it, he implies that God, specifically the Christ of Israel, would not have begrudged it — unless he was its exactor and follower, an emulator who would rather have discovered such faith in order to weaken and destroy it than to confirm it.

He raised the widow's dead son. This is no new credential; the prophets of the Creator had done the same, so how much more the Son? In that moment Christ introduced no other God, with the result that everyone there gave glory to the Creator, declaring, 'A great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people' (Luke 7:16). Which God? Obviously the one whose people they were and from whom the prophets came. If they glorified the Creator, and Christ heard and knew it yet did not correct them — indeed, in the face of such a stupendous proof, the resurrection of the dead, they were still praying to the Creator — then beyond doubt Christ either was not proclaiming any other God than the one he allowed to be honored in his own benefits and powers, or else what kind of savior would he be, letting them wander in error for so long when he came precisely to heal that error?

But John took offense at hearing of Christ's works, as if they belonged to another. I will first explain the reason for that offense, so that I can more easily demolish the heretic's exploitation of it. Since the Lord himself — by the word and Spirit of the Father — was working on earth and preaching, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit which had been operating in John in the form of a prophetic model should now withdraw from him, having been returned, as it were, to the Lord as its rightful master. Thus John, now just a common man, one of the crowd, took offense — but as a man, not as one who hoped for or understood another Christ, a Christ who had no ground for hope since he taught and did nothing new. No one hesitates over someone he knows does not exist and for whom he feels neither hope nor understanding; but John was certain that no God exists except the Creator, whether as a Jew or even as a prophet. It is easier to hesitate over someone you know exists but are unsure whether he is the one. That, then, was John's fear: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' He was simply asking whether the one he expected had arrived. For he hoped, as everyone thought, that judging by the similarity of the signs a prophet might have been sent in the interim, from whom another — greater — one would come, the expected one, namely the Lord himself. And so John's offense was this: he doubted that the one they expected had come, the one he ought to have recognized from the predicted works. Or did the Lord intend to announce himself to be recognized through those very works? Since those predicted works are consistent with the Christ of the Creator, as we demonstrate case by case, it is thoroughly perverse to claim that Christ is not the Creator's through the very things that compel recognition of him as the Creator's. It is even more perverse if Christ bears witness to John — confirming him as a prophet, indeed as more than a prophet, an angel — and cites the scripture about him: 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way' (Malachi 3:1), elegantly recalling the prophecy to settle the scruple of the offended John's question: 'Are you the one who comes, or should we expect another?' For once the forerunner has fulfilled his office, the Lord's way is prepared, and the one to whom the forerunner ministered is the one to be recognized. He is indeed greater than all born of women, but not therefore subject to the one who will be lesser in the kingdom of God, as if that kingdom belonged to another — a kingdom in which a lesser one would be greater than John, while another John is greater than all born of women. Whether he says this of anyone or of himself in humility, because he was regarded as lesser than John — since everyone flocked to John in the wilderness rather than to Christ — 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see?' — it amounts to the same thing: it belongs to the Creator that John is his, greater than all born of women, and that Christ — or any lesser figure who will be greater than John in the kingdom of God, equally the Creator's — will be greater than such a prophet because he was not offended by Christ, which is what diminished John.

We have spoken of the forgiveness of sins. The episode of that sinful woman bears on this: when she kissed the Lord's feet, drenched them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, she handled the solid reality of his body, not an empty phantom; and the penitence of the sinful woman, according to the Creator, earned forgiveness, taking precedence over sacrifice. Even if the impulse to penitence sprang from faith, through penitence justified by faith she heard from him: 'Your faith has saved you' — from the one who had declared through Habakkuk: 'The righteous will live by his faith' (Habakkuk 2:4).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the nuances of the passive voice (extollenda, scandalizabatur, iustificata) and the complex conditional/subjunctive structures. Scripture citations (Luke 7:16, Malachi 3:1, Habakkuk 2:4) are correctly identified and added to the English text as required by the instructions to match the quoted/alluded content. The title 'Faith of the Centurion' correctly names the thought of the opening argument.
